title: 3Sum
description: Sort, then for each anchor i, two pointers converge on the remaining pair. Skip duplicates at every level to keep results unique.

conversation.intro: How an interview about this problem would actually play out. Each section has two parts: what you'd actually say out loud, and why that move matters. Tap a section to expand.

sections.title: 1. Restate & clarify
sections.prompt: Before touching code — pin down the inputs.
sections.say:
"Let me make sure I have this right: given an integer array `nums`, return every unique triplet `[a, b, c]` where `a + b + c = 0`. 'Unique' meaning the set of triplets — order within a triplet doesn't matter, and `[-1, 0, 1]` should only appear once even if there are multiple ways to form it from the input."

Then a few quick clarifying questions:
• Can the input have duplicates? (Almost certainly yes — that's where the dedup discipline comes in.)
• Negatives, zero, and positives all allowed? (Need negatives for the sum to ever hit 0 with positives.)
• Any bounds on `nums.length`? (Affects whether O(n²) is acceptable — for n up to ~3000 it's fine.)
• Can I mutate the input by sorting in place, or do I need to copy first?
• Return shape — array of arrays, or some other structure? Does the order of triplets in the output matter?
sections.why: The 'unique triplets' clause is the load-bearing part of the prompt and the thing that turns a clean two-pointer scan into a problem with three layers of dedup. Surfacing it explicitly tells the interviewer you noticed. The mutation question matters too: sorting is the first move, and a real engineer asks before mutating someone else's array.

sections.title: 2. Brute force first (out loud)
sections.prompt: Name the obvious O(n³) solution before you discard it.
sections.say: "The brute force is three nested loops — pick `i`, then `j > i`, then `k > j`, check if `nums[i] + nums[j] + nums[k] === 0`. To dedup, I'd sort each triplet, stringify it, and put it in a Set. That's O(n³) time and O(n³) space worst case for the Set. Correct but slow — let me see if I can fix one element and reduce the inner two to a faster search."
sections.why: Two reasons to narrate this. (1) It anchors the O(n²) target as a clean improvement — you're collapsing the inner two loops, not reinventing the algorithm. (2) The brute force's stringify-and-Set dedup makes the in-place dedup-by-skip in the real solution look obviously better, which is what you want the interviewer to notice.

sections.title: 3. Spot the pattern
sections.prompt: What signal in the problem points to sort + two pointers?
sections.say: "Sum-to-target on an array screams 'sort it and use two pointers.' Here's the derivation: if I fix the first element `a = nums[i]`, the remaining problem is 'find two numbers in `nums[i+1..]` that sum to `-a`' — that's classic two-sum on a subarray. Sorting buys me two things at once. (1) Two-pointer convergence works: with `l = i+1` and `r = n-1`, if `nums[l] + nums[r]` is too small I move `l` right (bigger value), too big I move `r` left (smaller value), exactly equal I record the triplet. The sorted invariant is what tells me which side to move. (2) Duplicates cluster together, so I can skip them by comparing adjacent values — `if (nums[i] === nums[i-1]) continue` for the anchor, and after a hit `while (nums[l] === nums[l+1]) l++` and the symmetric `r--`. Three layers of dedup, all enabled by the sort."
sections.why: Pattern-naming alone is a guess. The derivation — fix one element, reduce to two-sum, sort enables both the convergence AND the dedup — is what scores. The bonus insight is that sorting does double duty here: most candidates pitch sort for the convergence and treat dedup as a separate problem. Calling out that it's one decision serving both needs is the senior move.

sections.title: 4. Trace through examples
sections.prompt: Walk a few inputs to confirm the model before writing the loop.
sections.intro: "Let me trace through a couple of cases to make sure my model is right." Three inputs cover the interesting behaviors — the canonical mixed input, the all-zeros dup-skip stress, and a no-triplet case to confirm we return empty cleanly.

examples.note: Canonical case — has duplicate anchors after sorting, so the i-dedup actually fires.
Dup-skip stress — every element is identical, the post-hit dedup loops are what prevent emitting [0,0,0] four times.
examples.trace:
sort → nums = [0,0,0,0]
i=0 anchor=0 → l=1 r=3
  sum = 0+0+0 = 0 ✓ push [0,0,0]
  while nums[l]==nums[l+1]: nums[1]==nums[2] → l++, l=2. nums[2]==nums[3] → l++, l=3. l<r false, stop
  while nums[r]==nums[r-1]: l<r false, stop
  l++ r-- → l=4 r=2. exit
i=1 anchor=0, nums[1]==nums[0] → SKIP
i=2 same → SKIP. (loop ends at i < length-2 = 2)
return [[0,0,0]]

examples.note: No-triplet case — smallest possible array (length 3) with all positives, so no sum can hit 0.
examples.trace:
sort → nums = [1,2,3] (already sorted)
i=0 anchor=1 → l=1 r=2
  sum = 1 + 2 + 3 = 6 > 0 → r--, r=1. l<r false, exit
(loop ends at i < length-2 = 1)
return []

sections.why: Two things the trace exposes. (1) The dup-skip loops on l and r need the `l < r` guard inside them — without it, on `[0,0,0,0]` you'd walk off the end and crash on the bounds check; the trace makes that very visible. (2) The outer bound `i < length - 2` (not `< length`) needs to leave room for `l = i+1` and `r`, and the `[1,2,3]` case confirms the loop exits cleanly even when the array is exactly length 3.

sections.title: 5. Edge cases to mention
sections.prompt: What inputs would trip up a careless implementation?
sections.say:
"Before I declare it done, let me think about edges:
• Empty array or length < 3 → `length - 2 ≤ 0`, outer loop never runs, returns `[]`. ✓
• All zeros `[0,0,0,0,...]` → exactly one triplet `[0,0,0]`; the three layers of dedup are what enforce uniqueness.
• All positives or all negatives `[1,2,3]` or `[-3,-2,-1]` → no sum can hit 0, returns `[]`. The two-pointer just walks out without ever finding `sum === 0`.
• Many duplicate anchors `[-1,-1,-1,2,2,2]` → without the `nums[i] === nums[i-1]` skip, you'd emit `[-1,-1,2]` three times.
• Large values near `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER` → `a + b + c` could overflow JS safe-integer range; for interview purposes I'd note it but assume inputs are bounded.
• Should I return triplets in any particular order? The standard answer (and what LeetCode expects) is that triplet order in the output doesn't matter, but within each triplet they're sorted ascending — which falls out for free because we read them off the sorted array."
sections.why: The dedup-related edges (all-zeros, repeated anchors) are where careless implementations fail — and naming each layer of dedup against the specific input that exercises it shows you understand which check is doing what. The integer-overflow callout is the senior touch; most candidates never think about it, and on a problem with summation it's a real (if rare) concern.

sections.title: 6. Complexity & wrap-up
sections.prompt: How would you defend the complexity claim?
sections.say:
"Time is O(n²). The sort is O(n log n) — dominated. The outer loop runs n times. The inner two-pointer scan for each anchor is O(n), because `l` only increments and `r` only decrements, so together they visit at most `n` positions per anchor. n outer × n inner = n². The dedup-skip loops don't change this — they're amortized into the same `l`/`r` budget.

Space is O(1) extra if we ignore the output array and the sort's stack (which is O(log n) for V8's quicksort). The dedup is in-place via the skip checks — no Set, no hash structure.

If you wanted to extend to 4Sum, it's the same template with one more outer loop layer: fix two anchors, two-pointer the remaining pair. O(n³). The general 'k-Sum' recursion is: peel an outer layer until you hit base case (k=2 → two-pointer), giving O(n^(k-1))."
sections.why: The amortization argument — that `l` and `r` collectively cover at most n positions per anchor, regardless of how many dup-skips happen — is the right defense against 'isn't the dedup loop nested inside the while loop another factor?' It's not, because the dedup `l++` and the main-path `l++` both consume the same budget. The 4Sum / k-Sum extension proves you see the template, not just this one problem — which is how the same shape generalizes.

notes: Sorting is what unlocks the two-pointer step — without it you cannot decide which pointer to move.
Three layers of dedup: skip equal i, skip equal l after a hit, skip equal r after a hit.
Outer loop stops at length - 2 so l = i + 1 and r still leave room for a pair.
reference.crux: Sort first, then fix each anchor i and converge two pointers on the rest — the sorted order tells you which pointer to move and lets you skip duplicates by neighbor comparison.
cruxDistractors: Three nested loops over every (i, j, k) triplet, deduping hits by sorting and stringifying each into a Set.
For each anchor, run hash-map Two-Sum on the rest for the complement −nums[i], then dedup the triplets afterward.
Sort, then for each anchor binary-search the remaining slice for the complement of each second element.

alternates.label: Sort + hash-set inner scan
alternates.when: A natural first step when you think 'fix anchor, Two-Sum the rest with a hash set.' Still O(n²) time but requires an extra O(n) set per anchor and an output-sort pass to guarantee deterministic order. Use when you'd rather not derive the two-pointer direction rule in an interview.
notes: The hash set finds the complement that was seen earlier in the scan — because the array is sorted, `complement ≤ nums[j]`, so each pushed triplet is already internally sorted.
An output sort is needed because hits for different anchors can arrive out of order; the two-pointer approach avoids this cost.
Same O(n²) time as the two-pointer variant but O(n) extra space per anchor for the set vs. O(1) with two pointers.

alternates.label: Brute force O(n³)
alternates.when: Only when you need to confirm understanding before deriving the faster solution. Three nested loops are correct but O(n³) — too slow for n > ~300. Name it out loud, then discard it.
notes: Sorting first means each triplet is already in ascending order, so the string key `i+','+j+','+k` is unique per distinct value-triple — a cheap dedup without sorting each candidate.
O(n³) time: each of the three loops visits up to n positions; even with early exits on anchors > 0 the worst case is cubic.
The Set grows up to O(n³) entries in the worst case (all unique pairs), though in practice it's bounded by the output size.

options: To collapse equal values into a single representative — the two-pointer scan then runs over uniques only
So two-pointer convergence can decide which side to move
So the inner loop can binary-search for the complement in O(log n)
To shift all negative numbers to the front, allowing a single-direction scan
O(n)
O(n log n)
questions.explain: Sort is O(n log n); the nested two-pointer loop dominates at O(n^2).

options: l moves right (bigger value)
r moves left (smaller value)
Both move
i moves forward
Skip anchors whose value cannot reach zero with any later pair (already known to be too large after sorting)
Skip duplicate triplets at the anchor
Reset the inner pointers l and r when the anchor's value didn't change
Avoid re-processing the anchor's mirror position from the previous iteration

questions.q: There are THREE dedup checks in the canonical solution. Where do they sit?
options: All three are at the anchor i, run before the inner loop
Skip duplicate anchors (i), then after a hit skip duplicate l values and duplicate r values
One at i, one at sum < 0, one at sum > 0
All three are inside the while-loop condition
questions.explain: Anchor dedup (nums[i] === nums[i-1]) runs in the outer loop; the l and r dedup-skip loops run only after recording a hit, before advancing the pointers.

questions.q: Besides enabling two-pointer convergence, what second benefit does sorting provide for 3Sum?
options: It removes all duplicate elements automatically as a side effect of the in-place sort
It clusters equal values adjacently, so duplicates can be skipped by comparing neighbors
It guarantees the resulting triplets emerge in lexicographic order, which the problem statement requires
It guarantees the inner two-pointer loop converges in O(log n) by enabling binary halving
questions.explain: Sorting groups identical values next to each other, which is exactly what lets the dedup checks work by comparing nums[i] to nums[i-1] (or nums[l] to nums[l+1]).

questions.q: Why is a hash-set approach messier for 3Sum than for Two Sum?
options: The inner Two-Sum's hash map must be rebuilt for every anchor, blowing the time bound to O(n³)
You still fix one element and Two-Sum the rest, but deduplicating the resulting triplets requires sorting/stringifying each one — work the sorted two-pointer avoids in place
Hash collisions are more frequent with three numbers because the implicit sum-key clashes with the pair-key
Hashing requires the input to be non-negative, so an extra pass to shift the range is needed
questions.explain: A hash approach finds the pairs but produces duplicate triplets, forcing you to canonicalize (sort + stringify) each triplet into a set; the sorted two-pointer dedups in place with simple neighbor skips.

questions.q: After recording a hit, why do the dedup-skip loops include the `l < r` guard (e.g. `while (l < r && nums[l] === nums[l + 1])`)?
options: To stop advancing once the remaining window is too small to form a valid pair complement to the anchor
Without it, on input like [0,0,0,0] the skip could advance l past r and read out of bounds
Because nums[l + 1] would coerce to NaN at the array boundary, breaking the equality check
To prevent the inner loop from recording the same triplet from the right pointer's perspective
questions.explain: On all-equal inputs the skip loop would keep advancing; the `l < r` guard stops it before the pointers cross and prevents reading nums[l+1] out of range.

questions.q: Why does the outer loop stop at `i < nums.length - 2` rather than `i < nums.length`?
options: The last two anchors can never sum to zero with any pair to their right, so they are safe to skip
Because l = i + 1 and r need to point at two more distinct positions, so i must leave room for a pair after it
The dedup check `nums[i] === nums[i - 1]` would index past the end at the last two positions
Sorted arrays in V8 are stored with two trailing sentinel slots that should not be read as data
questions.explain: A triplet needs i plus two later indices (l = i+1 and r); once fewer than two elements remain after i, no triplet can form, so the loop ends at length - 2.
